name: Even
confidence_why: The initial-stress coding rests only on the StressTyp2 (Goedemans, Heinz and van der Hulst 2015) and Gordon (2002) labels that trace back to Benzing (1955), which nobody has opened, while Novikova (1968, 1997) describes a weak, non-phonemic stress that usually falls on the last syllable or on a long vowel, Malchukov (1995) says the place of stress has never been studied, and Cincius (1947) has no stress section at all.
catalog_quote: StressTyp2 lect 106: pattern 112 summary 'In words of all sizes, primary stress falls on the initial syllable.'; passages 33 (Benzing 1955) and 159 (Gordon 2002) text=None; no words; no notes beyond 'ST0:fsa:notes:Main: 1L (all) Secondary: None (all)'. Gordon 2002 appendix p.541: 'Initial Even (Lamut) Altaic'.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's fixed: initial syllable coding (StressTyp2 pattern 112 via Benzing 1955 / Gordon 2002) only in the weak sense that it names no rival placement; it adds that stress is non-phonemic and that its position is unstudied, so it gives no support to 'fixed-strict initial'. It also does not contradict Novikova's final/long-vowel description (check note already on the record). The catalog quote is database-only with no primary text, and this primary grammar withholds any placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic (non-contrastive) in Even; the author explicitly declines to state its position or type, saying it has not been experimentally studied. No placement is given, so the source supports neither initial nor final nor weight-sensitive placement.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only qualification is that place and type are unstudied
new_statements.identity_note: Malchukov 1995 describes Standard ('literary') Even, which by his own statement (p. 4) is based on the Eastern dialects, in particular the Ola dialect of the Magadan region; the stress remark is made for Even in general. The Jazyki narodov SSSR 1968 chapter likewise describes the literary/eastern norm. The chapter author is not printed on the downloaded pages (pp. 89-91 + volume title page); attribution to K. A. Novikova is from the volume's known contents, not from the pages read.

readall_conflicts: Three-way disagreement. (a) The catalog codes Even fixed-strict initial on the strength of StressTyp2 pattern 112 (sources Benzing 1955 and Gordon 2002 appendix), with no primary quotation. (b) The only listed work, Malchukov 1995 (p. 7), states that stress is not phonemic and that its place and type have not been experimentally studied: it neither supports nor denies initial placement. (c) The Even chapter in Jazyki narodov SSSR vol. 5 (1968), which I opened as a bonus because it sits in the same Rosetta Project series (book p. 91 = p. 3, scanned), says verbatim: "Ударение экспериментально не исследовалось. Предварительно можно отметить, что в эвенском языке существует силовое ударение, которое значительно слабее русского и не сопровождается удлинением гласного. В словах без долгих гласных оно чаще всего падает на последний слог, в словах с долгим или дифтонгоидным гласным — на слог с этим гласным. Если в слове несколько слогов с долгими и дифтонгоидными гласными, то ударение падает на последний из них." [Stress has not been studied experimentally. Preliminarily one can note that Even has a dynamic stress, considerably weaker than Russian and not accompanied by vowel lengthening. In words without long vowels it most often falls on the last syllable; in words with a long or diphthongoid vowel, on the syllable with that vowel. If a word has several syllables with long or diphthongoid vowels, stress falls on the last of them.] This agrees with Novikova 1997:287 (already held b…

audit.recode_to: From fixed-strict initial to non-fixed / quantity-sensitive: 'stress on the syllable containing a long (or diphthongoid) vowel, otherwise on the final syllable; non-phonemic, not experimentally studied' (Novikova 1997:287, sec. 2.1.2), i.e. unbounded long-vowel-seeking with default-final, with a caution note that first-syllable short vowels are unreduced while non-first short vowels reduce (Tsintsius 1947:14; Novikova 1960 apud Aralova 2015:29-30), which is probably what the database chain read as 'initial stress'. Cite Novikova 1997 as deciding source; keep StressTyp2/Benzing as a recorded database contradiction.

tone.quote: В настоящей статье представлены результаты акустического анализа безударных гласных в двух агглютинативных языках – эвенском и эвенкийском. Безударные позиции гласных определялись согласно правилам расстановки ударения, представленным в работах по эвенскому [Лебедев, 1978 ; Новикова, 1991] и эвенкийскому языкам [Константинова, 1960]. [...] Полученные данные сравнивались с соответствующей статистикой по ударным гласным корневого слога в обоих языках. В результате выявлено, что, во-первых, количественно-качественная редукция гласного непервого слога оказалась общей особенностью в обоих языках.
tone.locator: p. 120; see also sec. 1.2 pp. 123-125 and Conclusion p. 128
tone.translation: This article presents the results of an acoustic analysis of unstressed vowels in two agglutinative languages, Even and Evenki. The unstressed positions of vowels were determined according to the stress-placement rules set out in works on Even [Lebedev 1978; Novikova 1991] and Evenki [Konstantinova 1960]. [...] The data obtained were compared with the corresponding statistics for the stressed vowels of the root syllable in both languages. It was found, first, that quantitative-qualitative reduction of the non-first-syllable vowel is a shared feature of both languages.
tone.says: An acoustic (Praat) study of stressed vs unstressed vowels that treats Even as a word-stress language — unstressed positions are fixed 'by the stress-placement rules' of Lebedev 1978 and Novikova et al. 1991 and compared with stressed root-syllable vowels; finds quantitative-qualitative reduction of non-first-syllable vowels; F0 is not analysed and tone is nowhere mentioned.
